name: King's Indian: Fianchetto
summary: The Fianchetto King's Indian (g3, Bg2) blunts Black's g7-bishop and takes a restrained, positional path prized as one of the soundest anti-KID lines.
intro: The Fianchetto Variation is White's most positional and one of the soundest replies to the King's Indian Defence, reached after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.Nf3 d6 5.g3 O-O 6.Bg2 Nbd7. Instead of building a big pawn centre with e4, White develops the king's bishop to g2, directly opposing Black's fianchettoed bishop on the long diagonal and reducing its influence. The whole approach is understated and harmonious: White castles, completes development and relies on smooth piece play and central control rather than a race of pawn storms. Black in turn prepares the thematic central breaks ...e5 and ...c5, and the resulting middlegames are quieter and more strategically nuanced than the fierce Classical and Sämisch main lines. It is widely regarded as one of the most reliable antidotes to the King's Indian.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 g6 Nc3 Bg7 Nf3 d6 g3 O-O Bg2 Nbd7

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The point of the g3 fianchetto is that the bishop on g2 neutralises Black's most prized piece, the g7-bishop, and reinforces White's grip on the central light squares, especially d5 and e4. Because White holds back from an early e4, the pawn structure stays more fluid than in the classical King's Indian, and the struggle centres on the d5-square and the timing of Black's freeing breaks. White typically completes development with O-O and then chooses a plan such as e4 with a big centre after all, b3 and Bb2 with pressure on the long diagonal, or Rb1 and b4 to expand on the queenside.

Black must decide which pawn break to base counterplay on. The move 6...Nbd7 prepares 7...e5, striking at d4 in true King's Indian style; alternatively Black can play ...c5 to hit the centre from the other side. Compared with the sharper lines, kingside attacks are harder to organise because the g2-bishop guards White's king so well, so Black more often seeks piece activity and central pressure. The positions are rich in manoeuvring, and small strategic details, such as who controls d5 and whether Black can achieve ...e5 under good conditions, tend to decide the game.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The classical main line continues 7.O-O e5, Black's principal freeing break. White then chooses how ambitiously to treat the centre: 8.e4 transposes into a big-centre position where after ...exd4 9.Nxd4 or ...c6 the game revolves around the d5- and c5-squares, while the restrained 8.h3 or 8.Qc2 keeps the central tension and invites slow manoeuvring. If White exchanges with dxe5 dxe5, the queens are often traded on d8, leading to a symmetrical-looking but subtly more comfortable structure for White that Black must handle accurately.

Black is not obliged to base play on ...e5. Two important sister systems, reached by a slightly different move order, are the Yugoslav Variation, in which Black meets the fianchetto with ...c5 and accepts a slightly cramped but resilient structure, and the Panno Variation with ...Nc6, ...a6 and ...Rb8, preparing the queenside expansion ...b5. Against all of these White's core idea is the same: use the g2-bishop and control of d5 to keep a small, durable edge and to steer the game toward positions where Black's kingside attacking chances are minimal.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Fianchetto Variation grew out of the same hypermodern ideas that shaped the King's Indian itself, with White adopting a Catalan-like g3 development to fight for the centre with pieces rather than pawns. It gained a firm reputation as a reliable, low-risk system through the mid-twentieth century and became a standard recommendation for players seeking a positional grip against the King's Indian.

Many leading grandmasters have used the fianchetto as a solid main-line weapon, valuing its blend of safety and lasting pressure, and it has long been considered one of the most theoretically respected answers to the opening. Its close kinship with the Catalan and other g3 systems means it appeals especially to players who like harmonious, strategically clear positions, and it remains a common practical choice at every level for those who prefer to avoid the mutual attacks of the Classical and Sämisch.
